units.title: Physical Quantities and Measurements
units.intro:
Fundamental SI: length m, mass kg, time s, current A, temperature K, amount mol, intensity cd. Derived: speed m/s, force N=kg·m/s². Prefixes: k=10³, c=10⁻², m=10⁻³, μ=10⁻⁶. Convert by multiplying by 1 in disguise (100 cm / 1 m).

Accuracy = close to true. Precision = tight repeats. Significant figures: measured digits you trust. Scientific notation: 3.4×10⁴. Scalar = magnitude only (mass, time, speed). Vector = magnitude + direction (displacement, velocity, force). Add vectors tip-to-tail or by components Fₓ=F cosθ, Fᵧ=F sinθ.

cards.title: 1.1.1 Fundamental and Derived Quantities
body: The building blocks of physics are physical quantities which are used to express the laws of physics.
Length, mass, time, force, speed, temperature, electric charge, and many others are physical quantities.
The three physical quantities - length, mass, and time - serve as fundamental quantities in mechanics - the branch of physics that studies motion and force.
All other quantities that are used in mechanics can be expressed in terms of these three fundamental quantities.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Systems of Measurement
body: In earlier times scientists from different countries were using different systems of units for measurement.
The three systems that were used were: the CGS, the MKS system, and the FPS (or British).
The units of length, mass, and time in the British system are, respectively, foot, slug, and second.

The slug as a unit of mass is not commonly used in the same way the kilogram is used in the SI system, because gravitational force, or weight, is commonly used instead of mass (pound instead of slug) to describe quantities of matter.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Metric (SI) Prefixes
body: For example, the diameter of an atom is 0.000 000 000 54 of a metre.
**A prefix** is a word or syllable that is put in front of a word to add to or change its meaning.
For example, 1/100 of a metre is a centimetre, 1/1000 of a metre is a millimetre and 1000 metres is a kilometre.
The same prefixes are used for other quantities.

lessons.title: Errors in Measurement and Significant Figures

cards.title: 1.2.1 Error, Accuracy and Precision
body: **Measurement** is the foundation of all experimental science and technology.
The result of every measurement by any measuring instrument contains some uncertainty.
Every calculated quantity which is based on measured values also has an error.
Systematic errors occur due to an improperly calibrated instrument or bias on the part of an observer.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Scientific Notation
body: Many quantities that scientists deal with have very large or very small values.
For example, the distance travelled by light in one year is 9 461 000 000 000 000 m.
Very small and very large numbers are best expressed with the help of scientific notation or powers of 10 notation.
Numbers expressed as some powers of 10 multiplied by a number between 1 and 10 are said to be in scientific notation.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Significant Figures
body: Normally, the reported result of measurement is a number that includes all digits in the number that are known reliably plus the first digit that is uncertain.
The reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit are known as significant digits or significant figures.
The length of an object reported after measurement to be 367.5 cm has four significant figures, the digits 3, 6, 7 are certain while the digit 5 is uncertain.

Clearly, reporting the result of measurement that includes more digits than the significant digits is unnecessary and also misleading since it would give a wrong idea about the precision of measurement.

cards.title: 1.2.4 Rounding off Numbers
body: The result of computations with approximate numbers which contain more than one uncertain digit, should be rounded off.
The rules for rounding off numbers to the appropriate significant figures are obvious in most cases.
The calculated area and the volume should therefore be rounded off to 4 significant figures.
Express its density by keeping the proper significant figures.

cards.title: 1.2.5 Dimensions of Physical Quantities
body: The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers (or exponents) to which the base quantities are raised to represent that quantity.
For example, the volume occupied by an object is expressed as the product of length, breadth and height, or three lengths.

Dimensional Formulae and Dimensional Equations The expression which shows how and which of the base quantities represent the dimensions of a physical quantity is called the dimensional formula of the given physical quantity.

cards.title: 1.3.1 Representation of Vectors
body: The magnitude of a vector quantity is printed in italic type (v is the magnitude of the velocity v).
When vector quantities are added, their directions must be taken into account.
Concurrent vectors: If all vectors such as, for example, forces may act at one point of an object, then such forces are said to be concurrent.
Coplanar vectors: If all vectors, for example, forces are in one plane, then the vectors are called **coplanar**.

cards.title: 1.3.2 Position and Displacement Vectors
body: Since the initial and final positions coincide, the displacement is a “null vector”.
Vectors, by definition, obey the triangle law or equivalently, the parallelogram law of addition.
Since, in this procedure of vector addition, vectors are arranged head to tail; this graphical method is called the **head-totail method**.
The two vectors and their resultant form three sides of a triangle, so this method is also known as triangle method of vector addition.

cards.title: 1.3.3 Addition and Subtraction of Vectors – Graphical Method
body: The lengths of the line segments representing these vectors are proportional to the magnitude of the vectors.
The addition of vectors also obeys the associative law .
Subtraction of vectors can be defined in terms of the addition of vectors.
The resultant vector R is directed from the common origin O along the diagonal (OS) of the parallelogram.

cards.title: 1.3.4 Resolution of Vectors
body: If vectors A and B are together equivalent to vector C, then vector C is equivalent to two vectors A and B.
When a vector is replaced by two vectors (in a plane, for example, xy-plane), the process is called **resolving the vector**, and the new vectors are called the components of the initial vector.
The components into which a vector is resolved are nearly always chosen to be perpendicular to one another.
The force F may be resolved into two component vectors Fx and Fy, where Fx is horizontal component of F and Fy is vertical component of F.

glossary.meaning: Length is the fundamental or base quantity used to measure distance or dimension in space.
Mass is the amount of matter an object contains.
Density is a measure of the compactness of the mass of an object.
Measurement is an inseparable part of physics.

tips.text: A Physical quantity is any quantity that can be measured.
Physical quantities are classified into fundamental (base) and derived physical quantities.

Each base quantity is defined in terms of a certain basic, arbitrarily chosen but properly standardised reference standard called a unit (such as metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela).
The units for the fundamental or base quantities are called fundamental or base units.
Physical quantities derived from the base quantities can be expressed as a combination of the base units and are called derived units.
A complete set of units, both fundamental and derived, is called a system of units.
The International System of Units (SI) based on seven base units is, at present, the internationally accepted unit system and is widely used throughout the world.
The SI units have well-defined and internationally accepted unit symbols (such as m for metre, kg for kilogram, s for second, A for ampere, N for newton).
Measurement is an inseparable part of physics.

Small lengths may be measured using a metre rule, vernier callipers, and micrometre screw gauge; beam balances are used for measuring masses; and stopwatches and stopclocks are used for measuring time.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: A person walks $$200\text{ m}$$ to the East, then turns around and walks $$60\text{ m}$$ to the West. What is the magnitude of the person's displacement?

steps.text: **Given:** Initial displacement $$x_1 = +200\text{ m}$$ (taking East as positive), subsequent displacement $$x_2 = -60\text{ m}$$ (West).
**Formula:** $$\Delta x = x_1 + x_2$$
**Substitution:** $$\Delta x = 200\text{ m} + (-60\text{ m}) = 140\text{ m}$$.
**Final Result:** The magnitude of the displacement is **$$140\text{ m}$$**.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Zahra travels by car a total distance of $$640\text{ km}$$ in $$8\text{ h}$$. What was her average speed?

steps.text: **Given:** Total distance $$s = 640\text{ km}$$, total time taken $$t = 8\text{ h}$$.
**Formula:** $$v_{av} = \frac{s}{t}$$
**Substitution:** $$v_{av} = \frac{640\text{ km}}{8\text{ h}} = 80\text{ km/h}$$.
**Final Result:** The average speed is **$$80\text{ km/h}$$**.

body: When no forces are exerted on an object or when the vector sum of all the forces is zero, the net force is zero.
If an object moves with a constant velocity, then the net force on the object is zero.
The forward force must be equal in size and opposite in direction to the force of friction in order to maintain constant velocity.
If there is no friction, there is no need for a forward force.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Newton’s Second Law of Motion
body: Newton’s first law describes what happens when the net force acting on an object is zero.
In that case, the object either remains at rest or continues to move in a straight line at constant speed.
In other words, an unbalanced force, or net force, accelerates or decelerates.
Newton’s second law involves force, mass, and acceleration.

cards.title: 3.1.4 Newton’s Third Law of Motion
body: Newton’s first and second laws explain how the changes in the motion of a single object changes.
Newton stated that a force applied to one object always comes from another object.
For example, the force of gravity on a falling orange comes from the Earth and the magnetic force acting on a metal nail comes from a magnet.
In other words, one force cannot exist without the other.

cards.title: 3.1.5 Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation
body: One day Sir Isaac Newton was sitting in his garden and noticed an apple dropped from a tree.
The sight of the falling apple made him think about the problem of motion of the planets.
Newton realised that the force on the apple must be proportional to its mass.
**Gravitational force** is a property of all matter; that is, every object attracts every other object with a gravitational force.

cards.title: 3.1.6 Normal Force
body: The cupboard exerts a downward force on the floor.
According to Newton’s third law of motion, the floor exerts an upward force on the cupboard.
The force that is exerted by a supporting surface on an object that is resting (standing, sitting, lying) on it is called the **normal force**, FN.
**Normal force** is a contact force between two solid objects and acts that is perpendicularly to the contact surfaces (e.g. cupboard and floor).

body: A ball rolling along the ground gradually slows down and finally comes to rest.

In all these situations no force appears to be acting on the objects, yet their speed gradually decreases and they come to rest after some time.
The force responsible for changing the state of motion of objects is the force of friction.

cards.title: 3.2.2 Advantages and Disadvantages of Friction
body: Car tyres are rough, so they provide high friction and prevent the car from sliding on the road.

cards.title: 3.2.3 Methods of Reducing Friction

cards.problem: Which of the following physical quantities is the correct SI unit of work?

steps.text: **Given:** Physical unit of work.
**Formula:** In the SI system, work is measured in Joules ($$\text{J}$$), which is equivalent to Newton-meters ($$\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$$).

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: A person carries a heavy suitcase of mass $$15.0\text{ kg}$$ and walks horizontally a distance of $$20.0\text{ m}$$ at a constant speed. The work done by the lifting force on the suitcase is:

steps.text: **Given:** Mass $$m = 15.0\text{ kg}$$, distance $$s = 20.0\text{ m}$$, vertical lifting force, horizontal motion.
**Formula:** $$W = Fs \cos\theta$$
**Substitution:** The upward lifting force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement.
Thus, the angle $$\theta = 90^\circ$$, and since $$\cos 90^\circ = 0$$, we get $$W = Fs(0) = 0$$.
**Final Result:** The work done by the lifting force is **Zero**.
